utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday we were still talking about Exhibit 1428, if we could have that on the screen. I don't know if you still have the hard copy, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the things you mentioned regarding that exhibit was that there was a map attached to it. Was the map attached at the time you signed 1428?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That map is an integral part of the orders pertaining to this action, that is to say, it has to do with this action. It was signed by the corps commander and it was approved by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question was: Was it attached to 1428 at the time you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, a map is made after the written part of the decision and it becomes an attachment. At the moment when I signed this, probably not, but what later the commander came by, signed it, and the units that were supposed to get this got it, primarily the 15th Motorised Brigade, that is to say both the textual part and the excerpt from the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little unclear on how this worked out. I understood from your answers yesterday that you signed this because the corps commander, General Pavkovic, was not available; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and in most cases that's the only possibility, otherwise the commander signs this. And when the commander cannot do it, then it is the Chief of Staff, his deputy who does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the order is dated the 14th and it contemplates action the next day, on the 15th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So where was the map then between the time you signed this document and the time the action took place the next day? Was it in your forward command post or was it in Pristina or do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall that detail, but if the Trial Chamber will permit me to explain how this functions, I am prepared to do so. You are asking me about where this map was. When the corps commander prepares his decision on a map, then it is taken to the army commander or somebody from the corps commander takes it or the corps commander personally. The commander of the army reviews it, approves it, signs it, and then it is returned to the corps command and is probably sent to the forward command post. I really do not recall. In principle, if it is a more voluminous map, then excerpts are made for units; if it is a small-scale action, then that entire map can be given to these units that are to carry out this assignment along with this written order for the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understood from our discussion yesterday that this was a relatively small-scale action, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that active -- activities were carried out by 15/3, that combat group that had less than 300 men. All the other ones had already been in those positions over the past several days on the basis of other decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, just as you had authority to sign the order in the commander's absence, did you have similar authority to sign the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would sign the map, too, had the corps commander not been at the forward command post at that moment, the army commander would have accepted my signature, too, that is quite customary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recall who actually signed this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recall, Your Honour, Mr. President, we showed it here as an exhibit, too, the map was signed by the corps commander, General Pavkovic, and he received approval for that by General Samardzic -- from General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were in doubt, Mr. Hannis, about the map, but you're clear that the map has been an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. I have a note here to check something to see if that's what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 5D1175 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if my colleague, Mr. Hannis, is looking for the map, it is 1174. I don't know whether it's a matter of confusion or whether Mr. Hannis is looking at something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we -- are we now to look at 1175 or 1174?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 1175 on the screen? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one you want, is it? Is that the one you want, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the one I thought was the map, but Mr. Bakrac indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's 1174 you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's 1175 I want. I want the map to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is this the map that you were talking about that relates to this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let him do it his way, Mr. Bakrac. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is this the map that relates to the decision in P1428?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see in the upper left a signature of General Samardzic, in the lower right corner the signature of General Pavkovic. Is there a date reflected anywhere on this map to indicate when it was signed or when the action was to take place? I don't see one, but ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber I wish to recall that we heard from one or two witnesses that decisions, or rather, map decisions the time is written. However, my experience is that in the decision there is no designation of time because the decision comes with the map. So the time has to do with the previously printed document that is called decision that has the exhibit number that you referred to a few minutes ago, but on the decision there is no time entry because it goes with the written part of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, why do you say the map is 1174?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a typo in my document. I created the confusion, so that is why I was on my feet, to apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General, then my understanding had been that typically the map and the written text of the decision relating to the action depicted on the map typically would be together, is that correct, so that whoever's dealing with it can look at the map and see if it accurately reflects what's in the text and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it seems to me that at the time that you signed the decision in 1428, under normal, standard procedure you should have had the map along with it, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First this document is signed, the decision, because it is the subordinate commander that drafts that; then the subordinate commander works on the map, but the map has to be verified by his superior, that is to say, there is a delay between the map and the written document. It is possible that the superior officer does not accept the map, does not approve the map, and then the written part of the decision will not be carried through either. That's the procedure of verifying decisions from the superior vis-a-vis the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm not intentionally trying to be thick here, but you said first the document is signed because it's the subordinate commander that drafts that, and then the subordinate commander works on the map, which has to be verified by his superior. So then the superior confirms the map by signing it in the upper left-hand corner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, in the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he signs -- in this case Samardzic signs after Pavkovic has signed the map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I understood from your previous answer that the document, the text, was drafted first before the map, and the text we have relating to this action is the one that's signed by you. Was that signed before the map was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that text is prepared at the moment the corps commander was not there, and then I signed it. The map was prepared, the corps commander came by, he signed it, it was taken to the army commander, he verified it, and all of it is in keeping with the procedure, to use that part of the unit for executing the combat task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So was the map then prepared at your forward command post, the same place at which I take it you signed 1428, they were both done at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably the case, but not necessarily. I have to say that to you, that's not necessarily the way it has to be done. Perhaps this map was done at the command post in Pristina, where the operations officer took it to the commander of the forward command post and then brought it to Djakovica to my forward command post, or rather, the command post where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm having confusion, because if the map is prepared and taken to Pavkovic, why couldn't the order have been prepared and taken to him at the same time? Why is he signing one and you're signing the other, unless the reason is is because you have been designated to be the one commanding this action, which is what Pavkovic told the Joint Command on the 13th of August. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there would be no need for General Pavkovic to sign this map, then I would have signed it, according to what you've suggested just now. And I assure the Trial Chamber that that has nothing to do with the actual use, with the army. I probably do not have the ability to explain command in this kind of action, so I'm refraining from speaking at too great a length. But I assure the Trial Chamber that this really has nothing to do with it, and it is not true that I was designated and that's not what that paper says, that I was designated to have this action under me, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, who could be better placed than you to have the ability to explain command in this kind of action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm prepared too, Your Honour, Mr. President; however, that's not the question that was put to me and I did not get your permission. But with your leave, I am going to explain this specifically. We have three levels of command here. If we look at this map, it has to do with small units, combat groups, up to 200 men respectively. This combat group is commanded by the commander of the combat group, with the rank of major or lieutenant commander [as interpreted]. He commands the action directly, and then he reports to the brigade commander, specifically the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade, his immediate superior, and that command is in Pristina. And the command of the 15th Brigade in Pristina reports at a third level, the corps -- to the corps command in Pristina, or to the forward command post in Djakovica, if there are some problems in the realization of this action from the point of view of coordinated action or the execution of the task in general. That is how the system of command functions in terms of the combat use of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My only concern was your claim that you did not have the -- well, according to the English translation, that you do not have the ability to explain command in this kind of action. Did you actually say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the interpretation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I just told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- But -- absolutely that does not correspond to what I had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have taken up so much time with something that doesn't matter as it turns out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just -- as long as we're dealing with the transcript, Your Honour, page 8, line - just to avoid confusion - it is line 16, he said with the rank of major or lieutenant colonel, not lieutenant commander. I think lieutenant commander is a naval rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, you don't recall if you saw the map at the time you signed the decision for the action reflected on this map, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that detail of having seen it at that time, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But that doesn't sound like the way that you personally would work, because wouldn't it be important for you to be able to see if the map and the text matched up with each other before the action was carried out?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I repeat this for the fourth time now. A written document is drafted, and then on the basis of that document - let me be quite clear - we make a sketch, so to speak, of that order on the map. It is plotted on to the map. And the map shows in a simplified manner what is explained in detail in the order, in the written order. The map is not the basic document. The basic document is an order, and the map maybe may contain more or less details. It is then used by the person actually carrying out the task, so to speak, symbolically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is the final decision that you signed, is that 1428, that's the final decision after you learned that the map had been approved?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid -- well, either I lack concentration to such an extent or interpretation is not good. The order is drafted, the decision is drafted, and then on the basis of this decision, the operations officers plot these elements on to the map. And then the map is signed by the commander and verified by his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if there are no corrections -- if the commander, in this case Samardzic, approves the map without requesting any changes or making any suggestions, then the draft decision ends up being the final decision, is that right, because you don't have to make any changes, what you drafted was shown on the map, there's no changes, so ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that's right. But I want to remind the honourable Trial Chamber that we've seen evidence here, exhibits, that even before that General Samardzic had made the decision with the basic contours as to who and how would carry out this action. He himself ordered that the 15/3 combat group would carry out this task, which is a little bit unusual for the army commander to designate a unit that has 300 men or less to carry out a task that is three levels below his level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that help you to understand the situation, Mr. Hannis, because I don't see that as an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that is an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, and it's become very confusing, this, and I would like again - I'm sorry to be clear in my own mind before we move on. Why have you referred to General Samardzic making or giving direct commands to the 15/3 combat group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, throughout 1998, for every day and for every use of any of the Pristina Corps units, the 3rd Army commander, General Samardzic, issued a task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there before we get further sidetracked. The question you were asked was a general question, which was whether if a draft is approved by the superior it effectively becomes the final order. That was the question, and you answered that by referring to Samardzic giving direct orders to the 15/3 combat group, and I don't understand the link between the general point and what may have happened on some other occasion between Samardzic and the 15/3 combat group. Is there a link?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I gave a very specific answer to the first part of the question. I said that it is correct. What the Prosecutor termed "draft" becomes -- that it then becomes a final version. I gave a very specific answer to that question, but I wanted to explain to the Trial Chamber that even before that this very same army commander did order all of that in quite specific terms. So I gave two answers, one that was asked of me and then I clarified. I don't know whether any of this is recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may assist you, perhaps you may want to look at 5D1174, Exhibit 5D1174, and everything will become much clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it will. I want to stress again to Mr. Lazarevic the importance of listening to the particular question asked and answering that particular question. And counsel, if they feel the need for more information to be produced either in cross-examination or in re-examination will raise the matter. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I rise with trepidation and at some risk I suppose. The matter is confused, Your Honour, simply because there's a lack of understanding. I can clarify it very quickly if you'd like me to; and if not, I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're talking about a lack of understanding of the general system, then I don't think it's for you to try to explain that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's lack of understanding of what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to that general question, to which the answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The progression was from an order by General Samardzic to then the preparation of the action documents for carrying out this order. All the witness was trying to say was Samardzic had already ordered this action way before he got around to signing the map; that's the point that he was trying to make, and I think that got confused somewhere along the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your evidence on this, Mr. Lazarevic, is that there were two orders, one by Samardzic and a later one that you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was Samardzic's order in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have it as an exhibit here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been exhibited and my counsel just referred to the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, and we had a witness, General Simic, who testified about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was actually trying just to get the mechanics of the process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course you're right and I don't depart from the instruction I've given Mr. Lazarevic, that he should answer the question that's asked. That's the way this system works, and he knows that very well from the time he's spent here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to persist a little bit, General. First of all, I just want to talk about in general the normal way that this works and then we'll talk specifically about this one a little more. And maybe it will help. Just imagine that you're the instructor at the military academy, I'm a brand new recruit coming in for training and you're explaining to me how these orders or decisions about actions are done. As I understand it, there's a decision made at some level, perhaps your commander, to carry out this action in Voksa. There's a draft made, it's written up, a draft about what elements are going to participate and what their tasks are, et cetera. Is that the first step?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then a map is drawn up based on that draft text, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me the next step.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next step is to draft the written part, the realization of the decision of the superior in the form of an order or a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I thought that's what I had said. There's a draft made, it's written up -- okay. So once you've done that, what's the next step?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision map is drafted, and it then has to be verified by the superior who had made the initial decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who's the person that does those first two steps? Who drafts the text, first of all, is that the subordinate?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the subordinate command, that would be the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who draws up the map, the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when that map is first drawn up, is it signed in the lower right-hand corner by the person who has drafted the map and is proposing it to the superior?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed by the subordinate commander, not the drafter, not the person who actually made the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then the map is presented to the superior commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Along with the text or only the map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly just the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if the commander approves the map as is, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the task is carried out in accordance with the deadline for the readiness that had been determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the original first draft of the text from which the map was created, what happens to it? Does it -- is there any change made to it to show that it is now final, or does it look just the same as it did the moment it was written before the map was created?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision or the order remains the same as far as the written portion is concerned, except if any interventions or amendments were made by the superior commander on the decision map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that means that the superior commander does not see the draft order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the draft order, when it was first prepared before the map was drawn up, is it signed by the person who created it, or is a signature only put on it after the map has been approved?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed once it is drafted. You don't wait for the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems to me that in that process there's some inherent danger that a first draft could go out as an original even though some changes may have been made by the commander after seeing the map. Isn't that -- isn't that a risk if you sign the original first draft?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written part is then made, an amendment to the decision or an amendment to the order, dealing with those specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you one more question. We talked yesterday about this, item number 6 talks about the Joint Command. And I think on the 6th of November when Mr. Bakrac was asking you about this he said: "Why does it" -- this is at page 17799, line 5. "General, why does it say in item 6 that the Joint Command for KiM will be in command of this action from the forward command post?" And your answer at line 9 was: "As there was a lack of concrete specific plans for cooperation and coordination which should have been done according to the Rules of Combat, the corps command decided in the last item which is dedicated to cooperation and coordination to use this expression in order to indicate that the action would be of common interest, of joint interest, and that cooperation and coordination would be in place between the army and the MUP and their forces." My first question is: Who in the corps decided to use that term "Joint Command" to express that this was going to be an action of common interest, of joint interest? Who was the person who decided that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is now the third time that's been asked; every time the witness has said he doesn't know. I don't know how many times Mr. Hannis can ask this question over and over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a very specific question, Mr. Ackerman, and I for one would very much like to hear the answer. It's not in terms exactly as posed before. Please answer the question, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my evidence so far I said that I didn't know who had made that decision, but that there were such documents originating from the corps command; and I explained what they meant for me, and I explained and showed on the document what they meant for the commander who actually implemented this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have more, Your Honour, or are you waiting for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't know who made the decision, how did you know the decision to use that term was by someone in the corps command, as opposed to some higher level or some outside level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the first page of this document, and it's the same for the Ratis action, that was a couple of days before, on the 8th of August, you will see that it says the corps command. That's what I'm talking about. I was physically away from the corps command, but this document, just as the one before it, is a document of the corps command. That's what it says in the letterhead of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you assume the decision to use the term "Joint Command" came from the corps command because it's in a document with the letterhead of the corps command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 5D1174 because it relates to this specific action. And as I recall from your testimony on the 6th of November, this was -- this is a daily combat report or a regular combat report, I'm sorry, dated the 14th of August, 1998. And in talking about this you mention that it was unusual for the army commander to issue a decision for a combat group which numbered 197 men. Do you know why this unusual step was taken by General Samardzic on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain that a few moments ago, too, that it was all the time the commander of the army who was making the decisions, that is his inalienable right. I said that it was unusual that the commander of the strategic group issues direct orders to lower-ranking tactical groups. He was in Kosovo at the forward command post, he decided, and that is how he commanded throughout. However, I cannot explain the reasons why that is so. That is his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference to it in this document, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure. We'll have to -- I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance, Your Honours. That is item 5 entitled "I have decided" and in paragraph 2 you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we'll ask if we can go to the appropriate pages in the B/C/S and the English which show item 5. Is it on that page for you, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Back one -- well -- we need to go back one in the English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I think to see the beginning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English we can now see the beginning on page 3, and I think we need, when you're ready, Your Honour, to go over to the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please go over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is that the reference to with BG-15-3, support MUP forces in crushing the DTS strongholds in the following sectors ..." That is what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I talked about, that is the decision of the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the only place it is in writing or is there an actual formal order by him to the battle group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no formal order within the daily combat report sent to the General Staff. The army commander made the decision, and at the evening briefings with the corps commander he defined this further, but I was not in attendance and am not aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then was -- who drafted then 1428 with the specific details of how this was going to be done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations organ of the corps command, one of the operations men, or a group of operations officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the forward command post or in the main command post in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the log number in this memorandum, it is my conclusion that it's the command post in Pristina and that this was brought to the forward command post. It's not the log number from the forward command post to the extent to which I can recognise it now, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if it was drafted in Pristina, why wasn't it presented to General Pavkovic for signature? Why was it brought to you in Djakovica? Isn't that because you were the one who was designated to command that operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic at that time was somewhere in the area of Djakovica with the Chief of General Staff. I was in the office preoccupied with the tasks I had because of this big team from the General Staff. And General Pavkovic went with the Chief of General Staff somewhere to the border. They were looking for him, they couldn't find him; I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it then the map must have already been signed by him somewhere else before he went out and about with General Perisic. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General explained at least five times that the map comes later. I think that this is intentional confusion of the witness. I did not react, but in response to three or four questions he says that the map follows after that. And now Mr. Hannis is saying that the map had already been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, it's not intentional. I am genuinely confused about this, and if it was signed on the 13th or signed on the 14th, I'm not sure when the map would have been done in time for the operations that were happening the next morning at 0700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your point is the order is signed on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the operation was on the -- the action was on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 15th in the morning, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's what 1428 says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We consider that the narrowness of the time-scale here warrants further pursuit of the detail of the order in which these events occurred, and we do not consider that Mr. Hannis has in any way deliberately tried to mislead the witness. The witness is able to deal with this issue, and we would find it of assistance for him to do so. So, Mr. Lazarevic, can you please clarify for us the position. Is there a possibility that the map was actually signed before the order itself was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the way combat documents are made. If you insist, whether that is possible at all, on some occasion perhaps yes; but I'm telling you that that is not the principle of creating combat documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a helpful answer to me certainly. The question is whether in this particular case, in view of the measure of uncertainty in your mind about the exact detail of all that happened, is it possible that the map was actually signed before the order was, also bearing in mind the fact that Samardzic had ordered the action in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, Mr. President, but the person drawing the map must at least have on paper a sketch of the information where he's going to send which unit. It's only the commander who makes that decision. He knows what he is going to write in the text, so he first draws the map and then writes the text. So he has the text and some elements from that text so that person who is technically drawing the map can include that in the map. That's why that is the order taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry that that has actually further confused me. My understanding is that it's an operations officer who draws -- who drafts the order, and that the commander was not available. So how are you saying the operations officer would get his instructions on what he was draft up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, that is the part that's been missing for this past hour, that I tried clumsily to explain. The preparatory part, the preparatory part for an action that is to ensue is a day or two or three days long, meetings, preparations, pre-planning as it is called, and then the operations man gets the idea of the commander, the concept of the commander, how and what should be done, and only then starts preparing this document. That is how an operations man functions, he has to get the basis from the commander or that is called the concept, the idea, of the commander in an outlined form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we know from Exhibit P1468 regarding the meetings of the Joint Command at page 54 in the English, we looked at this yesterday, and that meeting started at 2000 hours, 8.00 in the evening, on the 13th. General Pavkovic is telling the group, the Joint Command, that the -- that this action in Voksa would be under the Chief of Staff, that's you, that's the 13th at 8.00 or later that night. On the 14th of August, we see 5D1174, the regular combat report of the 3rd Army where Samardzic says with BG-15-3 support the MUP forces in crushing DTS strongholds. So when does 1428 get written up, also on the 14th, I assume because that's the date it appears on that document, correct? The 14th of --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, yes, that is what is written on the document, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the one that's signed by you, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now you told us before that that was prepared by the operations people in Pristina, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I infer that on the basis of the log number in the memorandum, in the letterhead of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But when you were explaining the general process to me earlier, you said the draft, unless there were changes made after the map was prepared, the draft becomes the final decision or the final order. It has a signature on it when it's prepared. So how did your signature get on it if it was prepared in Pristina? How did your signature get on it before the map was prepared, because you were in Djakovica, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let us be precise on this. Nowhere in military terminology does a draft order exist, a draft decision from a textual point of view. I accepted the Prosecutor's approach in order not to complicate the situation. So an order is prepared and signed; if there is a change, then an amendment to the order is made. A specific answer to this question, how. During those days since the team from the General Staff was there at the time, we were on the move all the time and probably somebody came to Djakovica and brought this so that the commander would sign it. General Samardzic was somewhere around too, probably; General Perisic was, I know that, they didn't find him. I signed it, and later on the commander signed the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A technical point, Mr. Lazarevic. Does that mean that if -- your answer about a draft, does that mean that if the superior makes a large number of changes, you don't tear up the order, you simply combine it with an amendment so that there are then two orders, the order and its amendment? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the supposition, as we call it in the army, the initial order would have to be revoked, it would not be torn up because it is already -- it has already been logged, and a new order would have to be drafted. But if that is not the case, then we only get an amendment to the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, a couple of points. I am trying to be precise here. You said just now, page 25, line 4, that: "I accepted the Prosecutor's approach in order not to complicate the situation." I ask you, sir: Don't accept my approach if you think it's wrong just to avoid complicating the situation because you're only going to complicate it more when you do that. I'm assuming that you understand my questions; and if you don't, you'll say so. And you said earlier that the draft was prepared and it was signed when it was prepared, and that was before the map was made. Isn't that what you said before, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not what you said before? Do we have to go back to the transcript and find it? You really don't remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little while ago, Your Honour, I explained that this was not a draft. The term "draft" does not exist. It's a decision, it's an order, but it is not a draft order. And this is what I meant when I said "approach." And I was merely trying to be accurate, precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that decision in the circumstance whereupon seeing the map the superior commander disapproves or makes amendments, I think Judge Bonomy was inquiring into this, what happens to it, because it's no longer valid, right? The superior has disapproved, made changes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you asked me if the decision is not approved, then there is no implementation. The unit is told that the execution of the task is postponed. If there are major amendments, I just explained to His Honour, a new decision is made and the previous one is revoked. If there are minor amendments, an amendment to the previous decision or order is drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let's see how you did it when there was an amendment to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, this will come up on the screen in a minute, but I know you're familiar with this one. This is dated the 22nd of March, 1999, and it's signed by you. I think the number from the Pristina Corps is 455-56/1. And in English the translation is "amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP forces in breaking up and destroying the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo." So is this the normal way an amendment would be done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, do you know of any other examples in documents we have in this case so far?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall at this point. I remember that instances when such tasks were revoked, when the army commander did not approve those tasks, this is in relation to what His Honour asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that amendment, you don't go through all the items that normally appear in that kind of decision, do you, because you start out with item number 4. You don't have 1 through 3, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't have some of the other numbers that normally appear at the end, including about who's going to command the operation, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we should look through all the documents. I see that item 1 is missing, items 1 through 3 are missing, and they're contained in the previous document. And I can't see now what items are contained in this amendment to the decision. I assume that there would be 11, because in the previous -- or to 13 because in the previous document we have 11 to 13 items.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go through the items of each in fairness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, can we go back one page to see if there's another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: See the last number we have apparently is 5.4. So we don't have the usual numbers that we have 6 through 11 or 6 through 13 that we've seen on many of the other decisions of this type, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that because as a matter of efficiency your amendment is only addressing those portions of the original decision that needed to be changed, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. I think there's a confusion and it's getting compounded. What is a decision? Do things move in a biplane, go to the apex, and then there's a decision after all the corrections and amendments and curative actions, which according to a policy are to be taken or would you also like to call things which do not reach the apex as yet remain in the pipeline through the -- through suggestions and through proposals, will they be also a decision? I mean, we have to really think what is a decision, and I think that would clarify things to a large degree. That's my humble submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I see you looking at me, Judge, I don't think I can answer that question, and I will address it with him. But if I may continue on this one a little bit and I'll try to follow-up to address your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't think you were able to answer my last question or didn't have the opportunity, but isn't that correct? You've only included basically items 4 and 5 because those were the only ones that you felt were necessary to change from the original 455-56, which by our numbering system is Exhibit P1966, dated also the 22nd of March? Isn't that right? There's no sense in writing over the entire thing 1 through 11 or 1 through 13? You're only making changes to items 4 and 5, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it is presented in the amendment to the decision, but I did put in a but. The previous document could not have been implemented because it did not contain the deadline for when the tasks would have to be carried out, so it was impossible to comply with it, to obey it. And that is the essence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's something that you put in your amendment, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the combat units that were going to carry out this action would need to have that first decision or order, 455-56; plus your amendment, 455-56/1; plus the map in order to be able to carry out the task, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't make any change to the original order, 455-56, which indicated that the actions would be under the command of the Joint Command? You didn't change that, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at the last page in the amendment to the decision, if we could look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not of this document, but the amendment to the decision. I don't know what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what we have on the screen is 1966, the original; you want to look at 1967, your amendment, and the last page, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought this was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've changed the order, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we're going back to 1967, Your Honour, the amendment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last line of this document, the amendment to the decision, the command post is designated in the Lausa village sector. The signature is that of the corps commander, and the commanders of the units that received this document have enough elements to be able to discern who the commander was and where the command post was where somebody from that command would be, would -- could be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see that, but you still haven't answered my question. You did not make any change to the provision in 1966, P1966, which indicated that the Joint Command was going to be commanding this action. You didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am explaining to you in military terms what this brief sentence means which has replaced the long one about who would be in command. As soon as you have this stipulation in a document, this constitutes an amendment to what was contained in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you not answer my question or are you just refusing to answer it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness is answering the question; that's exactly what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Bakrac --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand this view of Mr. Hannis's. I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not enough for you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness has explained the position as he sees it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's then go back. I had a couple more questions about 1428 and the sequence of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But I seek forgiveness in interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would request that some clarification is made in respect to the comment which I have made because in common workings there are inter-file notes, there are other things which just move from one desk to the other. Now, how could those be called decisions until they go to the apex and I think that is a bit of problem we are facing here because many things were being suggested, proposals were being made. Now, how could those be kept as something permanent? They may remain on the file but what value do they have. The ultimate thing would be a decision. And I think, I would request the witness to kindly just clarify this because a decision -- when is a decision? When a document will be taken as a decision? I mean that is important because then we know what is a decision. What is below that is not a decision, it's just a formulation of ideas which come from the bottom, go to the top, the hand-off, the department or the commander here or anybody could disagree with those, but what is ultimately decided is that at that stage not at the lower stage and we are discussing everything, even the inter-office norms, and that is why I think the whole thing is prolonging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can deal with this in two ways, Mr. Hannis, you can ask further questions if you can assist or -- yes. Is that something you could do?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's one other item I want to do with regard to 1966 and 1967 before I leave that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may be the way to do it is to encapsulate what your understanding is of the process at the end of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And see if you can do it in a way that the witness will confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, before we leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, before we leave these two exhibits, P1967 and 1966, I put it to you, sir, that you are trying to mislead me and this Court. You just now said that you made this change and the reference to command post in the village of Lausa is replacing what is said before about the Joint Command. If we can go back one page in this document, that command post in the village of Lausa, that refers to the command post for the 354th Infantry Brigade which has a task assigned to it under item 5.4. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, wait, you said remember --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if the Prosecutor remembers --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Yes. Let me ask you the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor is not allowing the witness to give a full answer. He said "yes, but," and the Prosecutor prevents him from answering in order to get a simple yes, and I don't think that this manner of cross-examination is fair. When the Prosecutor does not allow the witness to complete his sentence, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two questions in what the Prosecutor asked, the first question is: Are you trying to mislead me? And then the answer: Yes, would mean that the witness admitted that he was misleading the Prosecutor in this courtroom, and that is not proper, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's probably a linguistic point, because I certainly don't read the question and answer as amounting to that. So you need not concern yourself on that score, Mr. Fila. On the other question, though, Mr. Hannis, I think the witness should be allowed to explain. If it appears that the explanation is not addressing the point, then it will be stopped. Now, your answer to the question that the command post refers to the command for the 354th Infantry Brigade, you said yes and went on -- wanted to add an explanation. What is that explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at that command post of the subordinate brigade, parts of the corps command would be located. This is the usual manner of doing things. The superior command sends it command group to one of the command posts of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you then look at item 5.3, which has the task for the 15th Armoured Brigade. At the end of that you see "command post in the area of the village of Banjska," so there's a separate command post for the 15th Armoured Brigade. Were parts of the corps command also located there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The corps command selects a post from which it would monitor the situation and control the action. It cannot be in five places. The army commander was at my command post as his forward command post not at the Nis corps command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... There was a command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you were overlapping there. Please start that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In item 5.2 regarding the tasks for the 125th Motorised Brigade you'll see command post in the area of the village of Stari Trg. Were there any elements of the corps command at that command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, the essence of this action -- the brunt of this action is in Malo Kosovo. This is where the 354th Infantry Brigade is deployed. The corps command sends its command group there, not 150 kilometres away to the west where the 152nd Brigade is engaged in a task which is part of a larger task. So, Mr. Prosecutor, let me reply. Nobody from the corps command was at the command post of that brigade; they were there where the focus of the action was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more. Item 5.1, the tactical group 211, command post in the area Batlava. I take it from your earlier answers that no one from the corps command was at that command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So can you explain to me how reading this document one would know that elements of the Pristina Corps command are with the 354th Brigade in their command post at Lausa? It doesn't say that. How would you know that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post is in the village of Lausa. This is what is written here, and the command post of the 354th Brigade is in the village of Lausa, this is also what is written here. It's the same village, the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, what's written here is the command post for the 354th Brigade is in Lausa, but where in here is there any indication that the Pristina Corps command has elements there? There's no reason to think that they would be in Lausa instead of Banjska, Batlava, or Stari Trg, or Djakovica. How do you get that from this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last page, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General, I guess we'll just have to leave that for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's a minute early, but I'm going to move to try and address Judge Chowhan's point after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hopefully re-examination may assist on this because there is a separate command post referred to for each of these groups and the task they undertake in both orders. We shall break now and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, based on a comment that Judge Bonomy made just before we broke, I took another look at P1966 and 1967. One additional difference I saw is that in your amendment you have a task for the 354th Brigade which did not appear to be in Exhibit P1966. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the portion of the 354th that you were tasking in your amendment relates to a part of the forces specifically it appears to be the 120-millimetre Mortar Company and the 105-millimetre Howitzer Battalion, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not quite right what you said just now. By your leave, it says the 2nd Infantry Battalion in parenthesis, that that is the mainstay of this task. If you see 5.4 and then parenthesis, 2nd Infantry Battalion, without the mortar company and the 1st battery of the howitzer division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And their task is to support the MUP forces and in coordination with Tactical Group 211 prevent terrorist forces from pulling out. So why weren't elements of the Pristina Corps command also located with the Tactical Group 211 in their command post in Batlava?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hill of Laus and the Merdare and Prepolac passes that were supposed to be taken by the 354th Brigade with part of its forces dominate all of Malo Kosovo. From there, one can command and control and lead all units from the aspect of the possibility of maintaining communications and in visual terms too, if I can put it that way. That is where the observation post was too, where everything could be seen clearly how combat was developing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us before that the elements carrying out this action would have with them the map, the original order, and the amended order. Reading the original order and the amended order together, how would those elements know that they weren't supposed to be under the command of the Joint Command, because that's what the original order said and there is no specific direction in your amendment to indicate that that was no longer the case.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, as far as subordinate commanders are concerned, there was no dilemma on their part there. In response to your second question, page 2 of this document specifies the command post in Lausa and for every commander that was unequivocal, unequivocal for everyone who was in that line of work, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you said that 5.4 was the mainstay of this task. Do you mean that was the main part of the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this area where this unit was, practically one could control all forces. These are dominant features and Malo Kosovo spreads all the way from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no 5.4 in the original order. Does that mean that this was a very significant change that was being made by the amendment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. They're different units, but Your Honour, Mr. President, that order, that first order is without readiness. It does not say when the action would take place, and the question is whether it had left before that because readiness is not specified there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Hannis. Now, it's difficult, I hope you appreciate, for a layperson to understand how this second document, the amendment, makes it clear that part of the Pristina Corps command will be in that particular command post. That's what's causing the problem here. Maybe it's something that is intuitive for a soldier, but somehow or other can you get over to us why that would be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you say, I duly appreciate that a layperson cannot fully understand, but, Your Honour, Mr. President, I direct you to the last sentence on page 2 where the command post is specified, the command post in the region of the village of Lausa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lazarevic, every section of that order has a command post. If you go to the end of 5.3, it's got a command post; if you go to 5.2, it's got a command post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but for subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, as I said earlier, re-examination will clarify the point. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the command post in Lausa is a command post for the subordinate unit of the 354th, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, and at the same time -- at the same time of the command group of the Pristina Corps. Twice, the command post is repeated twice for the brigade and in the final part before the signature of the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not seeing that so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Neither am I, general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the problem. Perhaps there's something in translation that's causing the difficulty. It's only referred to once on the copy I've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, in the preceding point that refers to the 354th Brigade, its command post is stated, in the village of Lausa. When all the units were taken care of and when their command posts were set, at the very end of the decision the command post in the region of the village of Lausa is set for that part of the corps that is going to follow the action as it evolves. It is on the very last page on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it on the very last page and it is in exactly the same position in relation to 5.4 as a similar statement in relation to 5.3 and 5.2. Now, where's the additional reference to the command post in the village of Lausa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This last sentence, before the signature on the second page, the last page, it's probably page 2, pertains to the command post of the group from the command of the Pristina Corps because the command post for the subordinate units had already been set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you show me where it's set, please, for the 354th Infantry Brigade, 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the first page be called up again, please. Item 5.4, it says "task," and then the next page, please. In this part, no. Please, with your leave, could it be called up again. After the task is carried out -- but could I have a look at the previous page once again, please. The second subparagraph of 5.4, taking -- "the taking up of the zone should be carried out once our forces take over the broader region of village of Lausa, the hill of Lausa, trig point 630." That's the location, that's the elevation, below the pass where the command post of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not answering the question. Where is the reference -- the other reference to the command post in the village of Lausa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There isn't one in the sense of the village -- the command post village of Lausa, command post village of Lausa. In the first variant it is the village of Lausa and in the second variant it's the village of Lausa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I try one last time to ask you to explain how anyone reading this, be a soldier or anyone else, would know that part of the Pristina Corps command would be at that particular command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, because in the last point the command post where part of the corps command will be is determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have me defeated me moment, I'm afraid, but we'll need to move on, Mr. Hannis. We can't spend our whole lives on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I do want to ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1966, the original order to which your amendment pertains, item number 11 is command and communication and it says: "The Pristina Corps command post shall be in the building of its peacetime location." There's nothing in 1967 to say that that was changed, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written there, but with the leave of the Trial Chamber, there's this but. In every such document, order, and so within, that's the same thing that is written. We dealt with that yesterday, its peacetime location, et cetera, in all of those 14 locations, which is certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And so elements of the 125th or the 15th Brigades who were involved in this operation, how would they know, for example, if they had a communications failure and they needed to use a courier, how would they know that the corps command elements were co-located with the 354th in Lausa? They wouldn't, would they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the last simple sentence, to my mind they'd know on the basis of that; if not, they would look for another location. But I am saying that they would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to try and address the question that Judge Chowhan raised about the process. And this was the reason that I had used the term "draft" when I was talking about a first writing of an order or a decision relating to an action that's going to be written up in a map and then carried out. And if I understood the honourable Judge Chowhan correctly, the question is: When does that become effective as the decision or the order? Is it effective from the very moment it's written or does it only become effective after the map has been written and it's been approved by the commander? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a decision was verified on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And since there's nothing written on the map as far as the date or the time that that approval has been made, how would we know whether that first writing of the document has been approved? Do you follow that question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it becomes official once it's -- once the map has been approved, how do you know when that point of time is? We can't look at the map and see there's no time or date saying "approved" November 15th at 4.00 p.m. How do you know? Is that reflected in a separate document somewhere or does the subordinate commander just know because he's seen the superior sign it? How do we know when it becomes effective?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the subordinate commander, when he brings the map to his superior he provides a clarification, he explains it using textual documents, overviews, and data from the decision that had been written, decision or order. So he provides explanations. He doesn't just put it on the desk and says, Please sign that; he has to explain, justify, it for half an hour, for an hour using the data from the order or decision that had been written, using all kinds of overviews. And once the superior commander has heard him he says, Fine, I'm going to sign it. There is no special document. There may be a cover letter of some sort. That happens when somebody else, not the commander, brought the map for the verification, then there could be a cover letter saying, I approve your map and please proceed with the execution of the task. This is attached to the map that is sent back to the subordinate command, and with this cover letter which is very, very short, just a couple of sentences. When the subordinate command receives the map with or without the cover letter, it starts to work on the implementation of its decision vis-a-vis its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So until that time when the map is approved, what is the status of the written document? Is it just -- I used the term "draft," but you said that doesn't exist. Is it just a proposed decision? What is its status?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the decision of the subordinate commander which is there in a room. It is used by the organs of the command to draft their own orders and plans. They use elements from this order. They plot their own maps. They wait for the final verification from the superior command, if there is any need for them to add anything. So these processes go on in parallel. This order is there in this room, it is being read by the organs of the command who go on to draft their own orders; and the moment they approve, the map comes back, a comparison is made. And as soon as possible, the subordinate units start making their own supplementary documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if that's assisted Your Honour or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm very thankful for your addressing this, but there's another confusion and the confusion is because of the answer which doesn't elaborate another fact and which is that while the subordinate echelons are working with their own parallel maps on the basis of what the learned Prosecutor has called as a draft decision and then the maps get signed and the approval comes and that's the decision, but imagine if there are certain amendments made during the discussions which take place between the signing authority and the one who's explaining and he wants things to be done in a different way. Then what happens to the parallel actions of the lower command? Because they must be assuming that this will be approved, supposing that model is not approved and something happens, then what happens in that case? I mean, this I think the learned Prosecutor, this has not been clarified and I would request the witness to kindly throw some light on it because this can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that the interpretation of what I have said is not adequate. The organs of the command, not of the subordinate units, plan at the same time in the very same command that made the decision and took the map to the commander for verification. The other organs of that very same command have the obligation to make their own maps that are branch and service specific, and they have to enter certain documents, or rather, elements. And once the map that was signed comes in, the process of planning for that command is completed, unless there are any amendments. If there are any amendments, then all the plans will be corrected, amended, and if necessary will be drafted from scratch; and only then will subordinate units be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, your description of that, General, reminds me of a situation that we've had some evidence about regarding Exhibit P1487, which were the suggestions from General Ojdanic regarding a Joint Command order that's in Exhibit P1868 or 1878. Do you recall when General Curcin testified here about that event and how the suggestions came to be created? Do you remember his testimony about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And let me know if your recollection is generally the same as mine regarding that event. I don't have the specific page reference in front of me but I think he said he was called in by General Ojdanic, who had a map, and told General Curcin this is something he received from General Pavkovic, who brought it in after having met with the supreme commander Mr. Milosevic. And that from looking at that map General Curcin and General Ojdanic, even though they didn't have the decision, the text decision, they were able to write up some suggestions which then were sent down the line. Do you agree with me so far, that that was his explanation of how the suggestions were created?
