utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understood his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe Mr. Ackerman introduced an exhibit, 4D420, which is from General Pavkovic after the event, advising General Ojdanic that had not been able to carry out the suggestions, partly because there was a delay in receiving the information and I think also because it was -- he described it as a MUP operation rather than a VJ operation. But doesn't that incident reflect a flaw in the system if the original text can be treated as a valid order even while you're awaiting approval from the superior commander in the form of his signing off on the map? Because Ojdanic wanted to suggest some changes, but the operation went ahead without his approval. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to be able to say -- not to say yes or no but to explain the way I understand it. To my understanding, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff did not approve this decision. This was not his level. This was not something that he planned. This was planned at a lower, tactical level, at the level of the corps command and partially at the level of the army command the way I understand it. He was not involved, or rather, the Supreme Command Staff was not involved in the planning of this, and this is why my answer to you is no, this is not so. But on the other hand it is quite legitimate for the Chief of the General Staff, or rather, the Supreme Command Staff when he sees a situation and when he feels that amendments can be made may intervene, even though he did not take part in the planning process and in the decision-making process in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, did not General Curcin tell us on that map in the upper left-hand corner were the words "Joint Command" and no signature, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard his testimony this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The suggestion I think, Mr. Lazarevic, is that while the Supreme Command Staff may not have had a role in the authorising of that operation, that perhaps the supreme commander did. But you're telling us that it was an action planned at a lower level but was also authorised at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was planned and authorised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who authorised it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was authorised by the 3rd Army commander. The corps planned it; the 3rd Army commander authorised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your basis for saying that the 3rd Army commander authorised it is because he's the one who brought the map to Ojdanic, or is there some other basis for that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My basis is my personal involvement, experience with the -- with using the corps during the war, and the 3rd Army command with its forward command post was at the corps command post. And the corps did not carry out a single action without the knowledge of the army command, and the army command always reported to the Supreme Command Staff on all those actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, could we look at exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I don't know what action Mr. Hannis is actually referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I was just asking if we could look at Exhibit P1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I have been referring to the action that is described in the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija order which bears that number 455-148. And you'll recall from the testimony that that is the number that is referred to or linked to in General Ojdanic's suggestions in Exhibit P1487. Will you accept my word for that or do I need to show you 1487?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in answer to my previous questions -- actually, I understood you to be asking me about that, that that's what you were referring to, and that's the way I took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you see now on the screen P1878, which is that order, to break-up and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the Rugovo sector. And this is another one of those unsigned and it just has at the end Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. So based on your earlier answer that this came from the army command, what's the relationship between General Pavkovic, as 3rd Army commander, and the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say, as far as I can recall, that this originated from the 3rd Army. This log-book number is the log-book number from the corps command. I merely said that everything that was done in the corps was verified right there on the spot and was reviewed and then implemented. And I really don't recall having said that this originated from the 3rd Army, which does not mean that the operations officers from the 3rd Army who were at the forward command post did not work on this document together with the operations officers from the corps. It would have been wrong not to have done so, but I explained that this log number 455 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, I was looking at page 48, line 6, in your answer to Judge Bonomy's question about who authorised it, you just told us: "It was authorised by the 3rd Army commander. The corps planned it; the 3rd Army commander authorised it." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That makes it a Pristina Corps action, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then what is the connection between the Pristina Corps and the Joint Command if this was planned by your command and approved by your superior, General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In factual terms, there was none. There could not have been one. In technical terms, what does this title have to do in this document? Let me repeat, Your Honours, by your leave. This is an indication of the form of the coordinated action and combined command in the execution of a general task between two structures, the army and the police, which have the same task, but where each structure retains its own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And looking at the description of the task in this order, would you characterize this as a MUP operation or MUP action?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document you can see the specific tasks for a small, small part of the Pristina Corps, it's a small force that is supposed to support the MUP in the action to deblock the Rugovska Klisura area from the terrorist forces. This is the essence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you have any idea why a small action like this is something that would be brought to the attention of apparently the supreme commander and the chief of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really don't have the information that the supreme commander was involved in it. He may have received some information about what was going on, but that's not something that I know of. As -- and now as to why the chief of the Supreme Command was involved, well the Supreme Command Staff was interested in the overall situation in the 3rd Army, and in particular in the Pristina Corps. They followed the events in -- on the map. We heard people from the operations centre who testified here. It is quite logical for me for the Supreme Command Staff to be interested in knowing that a light infantry battalion was trying to carry out some task in some gorge somewhere or other. For me, this is absolutely acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the Pristina Corps command, can you give us the names of the individuals who prepared this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there are no initials here, I can only say with a considerable degree of certainty that these would be the operations organ, Colonel Stefanovic, as he was at the time; Colonel Tesevic; sometimes Colonel Paprica. So that was the group of people at the corps command who were involved in the planning process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is it fair to say it would have been at least one of those three that was involved? You may not be able to tell us precisely which one, but those were the guys who did that kind of work and it would have been one of them. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to say that Colonel Stefanovic was responsible, he was at the head of this organ; but whether he did this or some of his subordinates, I really can't tell. But he was responsible for drafting this, that was Colonel Radojko Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move away from that for now and take you back to your first day of testimony. You were shown a video by Mr. Bakrac at page 17773. This was a video I think you told us was from January or February 1999, showing what appeared to be what you described as the terrorist forces in uniform with weapons Marching through the snow and apparently doing some training or exercising. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned this was an example of what you were aware of about the severe problem of large groups of terrorist forces and armed rebellion forces and insurgent forces throughout Kosovo. Did you advise the -- well, first of all, when did you see this video? I don't recall if you told us when you first saw it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this video recording, I saw it after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But you told us you did have other data about large groups of terrorists between 400 and 600 villages, where there were at all times terrorist forces and insurgent forces. Did you inform - and when I say "you," I mean you in the army - did you inform the MUP about this intelligence? Did you share that information with them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information were exchanged through regular intelligence security channels, but they were also transmitted to the international representatives of the OSCE mission, which to my mind is also important. As for the MUP, yes, as well, with public and state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think your testimony was that after the OSCE KVM mission arrived, that you - you, the army - weren't attacking any of these terrorist strongholds, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, unless there was a direct attack from those locations against the army; then there would be a response to the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the MUP, weren't the MUP doing operations against some of these strongholds during this time-period, after the KVM arrived?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the MUP had strictly defined locations where they could be. These were the so-called points, 20 or 27, where they secured the area and communications. I really do not have information about the MUP carrying out some active activities vis-a-vis the rebels, such as actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you were aware of the action at Racak in the middle of January 1999, right, that was a MUP action?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, yes. That was an action, an attempt to arrest persons who had previously killed a few policemen. This action assumed wider proportions practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the 549th Brigade under I think it was Colonel Delic at the time, were you aware of actions that they took part in in conjunction with MUP personnel in the middle of March, say the 12th of March and the 18th of March, before the war started?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the border belt, as far as I can remember, towards Albania two anti-terrorist actions were taken, Jeskovo and Kabas. This was previously announced to the OSCE mission, that there were terrorist forces there who were jeopardizing accessibility in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And accessibility in the border belt, in what way do you mean they were jeopardizing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite specific, the village of Jeskovo that was vacated, there were no civilians there, it was turned into a classical terrorist stronghold of the FARK type. They cut off the road to Dragas, and at the Dragas plateau there were five border posts of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Pristina Corps, and they became inaccessible. As for Kabas, directly above the barracks they also moved out the civilian population and they prepared an attack on the very barracks of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was Prizren in the Prizren barracks within the border belt?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Prizren, but the village of Kabas and Korisaje [phoen], that area where the concentration was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You showed us a map, Exhibit 5D1334 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have that up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Page 17775 you told us that this was made in the operations organ, together with the security organ of the Pristina Corps. And I think you described this as a survey map of the armed Albanian villages or -- yes, the armed Albanian villages in Kosovo and Metohija from 1998 and 1999. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said that you thought it was created in February 1999. I have a question about exactly what time-period does this cover. If it was created in February 1999, how far back in 1998 does it go, as far as reflecting the location of armed Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the month of April 1998 up until the end of the war, this part pertains to the month of February when there was an escalation. There were other maps, too, in terms of the broader regions without this micro-regionisation according to information on what village had received weapons or where these forces had come. Then these locations were marked, information was updated, and this is the so-called review map. That is what it is called, or rather, the overview map, as it is called in military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, the thing I'm trying to understand is that one of these blue dots I take it may have been put on the map because of information you had that that village was armed in May of 1998, for example, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, starting from April onwards. Some later some earlier. This is what the situation was in the month of February, 1999, but a very large number, over 400, that is the information from the other side if I may say, 406 is KLA information. Of course not all of that was portrayed, it cannot be portrayed on a map this big.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm confused because it says 1998/1999. Is it your evidence that every blue dot on this map reflected an armed Albanian village that was armed in February of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That in February 1999 constituted a terrorist stronghold.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then why doesn't it just say "February 1999"? Why the reference to 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this overview map was kept from April 1998 and it was added upon once additional information was received in terms of attacks against the security forces or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. It was added on. But were any of the dots removed, because you know in -- starting in July 1998 through the end of September 1998, it was a big operation, part of the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism, in which a number of villages were the subject of joint actions by the MUP and the VJ, and including a number of actions or - for lack of a better word - operations in which villagers were surrendering their weapons to the army and the MUP. You knew about that, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. Some villages practically became passive, voluntarily surrendered arms, but already from the month of October onwards when the OSCE mission came. Regrettably, yet again there was this forced mobilisation of an even larger number of Albanian villages. It is possible that some of the villages from April or May 1999 were not shown here because they evaded forced mobilisation, if that is what your question was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, my question is that I would suggest to you that a number of these blue dots as of February 1999 were no longer armed Albanian villages, either because the villagers had been driven out or they had surrendered their weapons, et cetera. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true for a simple reason. Because the number of terrorist acts from October, especially from January and February, was doubled in Kosovo and Metohija, attacks against civilians, the army, and the police. I am talking to you about what in fact happened in Kosovo and Metohija. This was carried out by those forces relying on these strongholds and these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that connection we've seen a document, I think it's Exhibit P2808.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, you'll recognise this. I think it's from the 16th of February, 1999, and it's signed by you. And the English translation title is: "Order to break-up and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo." You're familiar with this, yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In preparing this document, did you rely on information in that map that we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an overview map this is a more lasting one, that lasts longer. Specifically for this action the most recent verified data from the operative zones of brigade were used, or rather, the operative zones of the armed rebellion forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say there that one was an overview map and the other was more lasting, because there seems to be a mistake in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map that was on the screen a few moments ago is an overview map which lasts longer, which is used for a general picture and for following the situation; and when embarking on a specific action, then one verifies and collects concrete data from the ground, from subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought, Mr. Lazarevic, you had told us that the operation up until end of September into October 1998 was very successful and largely overcame the terrorist threat at that stage. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it seems odd that we should have a map with the location of villages with significant terrorist presence that covers the period April until February. I mean, it can't have an accurate picture, surely, as at February unless it's been amended to reflect the changes in circumstances during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map from the month of February that contains numerous locations from 1998 as well and new locations, too, in terms of focal points of rebellion. Because from October to February - and we've also heard testimony of those who led this armed rebellion - they achieved more than during the summer offensive of the Serb forces, as they had said, in terms of territory control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but it doesn't automatically follow as a matter of logic that the same villages are occupied by terrorist forces. And the period in time that really matters for us is what the situation was in February. And really, this map doesn't tell us, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, this is the situation in the month of February, but I'm telling you specifically as well Junik, may I give an example, one example only. Junik in 1998 was a centre of the armed rebellion. It was Junik with the surrounding area that was a centre in 1999 as well, not to go into other examples. Jablanica and so on. I don't want to take up your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this map prepared for the purposes of the trial, since you hadn't seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say, Your Honour, that I had not seen it. I said ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that this map, as far as I can recall, was made in the corps command, the overview map I mean, on the basis of the maps that were kept by the operations organs and the security organs. And they cover larger areas of the deployment of the forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when did you first see this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first saw this map in February and March, until the beginning of the war, and I looked at it several times in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was confusing your answer about the video with your answer about this. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, the question that I have from that previous discussion was: But as of February 1999, that map is not entirely an accurate picture regarding location of armed Albanian villages because by that time some of those villages that may have been armed in April or May or June of 1999 were no longer armed villages. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my answer. Unfortunately, it was not correct - but not from that aspect - because the terrorist forces were much larger than what we had assessed and that we had forecast as to the developments that would follow. We assessed that there were 17 brigades and there were over 22, 25 brigades, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And because it wasn't accurate, you did not rely on it in preparing Exhibit 2808, your 16th February 1999 order, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that as far as this particular order is concerned, that the data had been verified, the security data at the corps command and also the data from the subordinate commands because this is a specific order, and certain anti-terrorist action was to be carried -- a quite specific counter-terrorist action was to be carried out on the basis of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question is: You did not rely on that map, did you, in preparing your order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did and we [as interpreted] did not. This is an overview map. This is a document that is there to assist us, it's an aid, and this is something that you monitor every day. You plot things on it. But if you want to launch an action, you have to check. If a terrorist unit enters a village, takes it, and is there for three days and then leaves, this is something that you have to monitor. You have to follow these developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer has been recorded as: I did and we did not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: I did and I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say "I did and I did not"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we did use this map in part, but we did not, but from the point of view of preparing for a specific action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I can understand it would make sense to use the map if you were updating it on a regular basis and if you got information about now on February 10th, there's another armed village over here; and on February 15th, there's another one here, and you put another dot on the map. But from what I can see from the map is that all the dots are the same colour and there's no way to know whether that dot was put on in April 1998, or last week, in February 1999. So how does that help you plan your operation when you don't have a time-line or anything to indicate to you what the status is today, in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the witness has just replied and you took him back. You were not clear what he meant when he said yes and no. It's an overview map, but if a specific task is given, then further checks are made to verify its accuracy and the witness said that loud and clear. I don't know why my learned colleague Mr. Hannis is now bringing him back to it, and the question was whether he used that map, and I think he explained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is related to the usefulness and the -- of the exercise and the accuracy as at February 1999 of the map; and therefore, we shall repel the objection and allow the witness to answer the question. The question was: So how does that help you plan your operation when you don't have a time-line or anything to indicate to you what the status was of these villages at February 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a map from February. It was not made in a single day. It was based on the intelligence gathered in the previous period, and it shows where the main force and where the flash-points of the armed rebellion were as of February 1999. Those flash-points tally for the most part with the ones in 1998. So this map shows that in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, that's creating more uncertainty in my mind, Mr. Lazarevic. If this was compiled in 1999 and the purpose of it was to show the position as at February 1999, what's the point in looking at the situation in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is a confusion here in this whole question and answer thing, because the Prosecutor asked me: When did such overview map came into being, when did it start to be plotted. I said it was in April. But this map depicts the situation as of February 1999, and let me just give you one more sentence. This map was accompanied by a textual overview with the names of the villages and municipalities and there were indications next to the villages whether they were armed, whether they were terrorist strongholds, and this was updated, this textual overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you waiting on me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me move on to something else. Your exhibit 5D1370 was shown to you by Mr. Bakrac on the 6th of November to help explain to us the organizational structure of the Pristina Corps. I have another document I want to show you that's similar, this is Exhibit P2556. This is something that was prepared by the OTP and it purports to show some or most of the units that were under the Pristina Corps at the time. Now, I realize it doesn't match up identically with yours and certainly defer to your document. But what I wanted to ask you in connection with this one is if you can identify for us the commanders of some of these brigades or subordinate units. We did not have a name for a commander for the 252nd Armoured Brigade. Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milos Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the 72nd Special Forces Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be allowed at this point to say that 72nd Special Forces Brigade was not in Kosovo and it was not subordinated to the corps. There were two smaller elements, a hundred men each, and I perhaps would not be very accurate in my answer because I would be just guessing. That man was not in Kosovo, whether this was Colonel Cvetkovic or somebody else, and that's why I can't give you an answer. It says here the 72nd Brigade and that brigade was not in Kosovo and Metohija as a brigade and its brigade commander was not in Kosovo. That's why I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander was for those elements of the 72nd Brigade that were in Kosovo in 1999? Do you know who their commander was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this combat group that we call the Anti-terrorist Battalion, it was Major Markovic, he was the commander and as for the combat group of the reconnaissance battalion, I believe it was Major Dunjic. When I say "I believe," I mean to say that I'm not quite certain as to the accuracy of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. How about the 52nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Stevo Kopanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 52nd Reconnaissance and Diversionary Company?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember who was the company commander. I really can't tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And just two more, the 53rd Border Guards Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Dusko Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 57th Border Guards Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sveta Antanasijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I want to go to Exhibit P1085. I think I need e-court page number 145 in the English and 144 in the B/C/S. I'm looking for paragraph 450. General, this should be -- if my notes are correct, this should be the VJ Rules of Service. I appear to have the right page in English, but I may need some help on the B/C/S. I don't know if Mr. Bakrac can assist. I'm looking for Article 450. I see --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At least we have the beginning of it. General, you recall testifying about this earlier? This is a section that talks about the use of the units and facilities or installations in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Article 450 talks about: "Army units may be used to fight insurgent, sabotage, terrorist, or other hostile armed groups or to prevent and eliminate a state of emergency in accordance with a decision of the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Supreme Defence Council." Now, am I correct in reading that where it says "to prevent or -- prevent and eliminate a state of emergency"? I'm thinking hypothetically, but it seems to me that if I were the supreme commander of the army I could argue that any use of the army at all was to prevent a state of emergency. If there were ten students demonstrating on the corner, I might say, Bring in the army and arrest those students because I want to prevent a state of emergency. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I understand this paragraph, 450, of the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia in peacetime because some other tasks are listed here before this. And as far as I understand a state of emergency, the way I understand it as a citizen of that country, I understand it in completely different terms. I see it as a state that endangers the overall security in the broader region or the -- it is something that poses a severe threat to the country and to the constitutional order. And I would not agree that a dozen students would pose such a threat to the security of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would agree with you, that that in my mind wouldn't pose a threat to the country. But you see how that wording leaves it to the discretion of those, that is, the president of the Federal Republic, or those members of the Supreme Defence Council who are making the decision; it leaves the discretion to them, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I really can't give you an answer to this question because it is an issue of constitutional law, and I'm sorry that I can't give you an answer that you're expecting from me. I've just told you what I take the state of emergency to mean as a citizen and as a military officer. Now, as to who decides on it, this is not a discretionary right. It is quite clearly stipulated, but this is not really my field and I really can't assist the Trial Chamber about an interpretation of a state of emergency in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you told us on the 6th of November at page 17782, line 2: "As a citizen of the country, not to mention as a soldier, when I know that 50 per cent of the territory of the province of Kosovo and Metohija is blocked by armed rebel forces, that is the most severe state of emergency that can exist in a country. And the fact that the state has not decided to declare a state of emergency is up to the state organs, but it doesn't affect the need to use army units to eliminate the threat." So it was your position in early 1999, wasn't it, that a state of emergency actually existed in Kosovo, even though it had not officially been declared by the state authorities, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the State of Serbia, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the constitution and some other laws, I will not be enumerating them, define what the state of emergency is and who declares it, and I gave you my view. And I think to this day that it was a disaster for Serbia and for the state as a whole, but I merely gave you my view as a military officer. It is not up to me to say why somebody did or did not declare a state of emergency. For me, it is a state of emergency when you -- when people are getting killed every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall break now and resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, just before we broke we were talking about your answer the other day in which you described the extreme situation in the country and how in your view that was the most severe state of emergency that can exist. It sounds to me like you would have agreed with General Perisic, that a state of emergency should have been declared back in the late spring or early summer of 1998, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can say that I agree or disagree with my second or third superior that time, but at that time, as an officer, I was saying what I thought. And I think -- well, now with your leave and with the leave of the Trial Chamber, actually, I think you want to hear what it is that I think, whether indeed a state of emergency should have been imposed or not. As a soldier, on the one hand I thought that should have been done. But I truly was aware, since I was in Kosovo and Metohija, that the state had not decided on that because there was a real danger of this internal conflict escalating very, very fast into an international conflict. Secondly, the imposition of a state of emergency in Kosovo and Metohija would have wider implications in terms of inter-ethnic relations because practically the democratic rights of citizens are suspended, and this has to do with a vast majority of the population. So I think that it's these two reasons, not to go into any others, at that time did not allow - well, this is my assessment - the state leadership to take that kind of decision, but rather, to try to prevent a further escalation of the conflict and an even worse state of emergency by engaging security forces at a given point in time to eliminate these major dangers. This is my assessment, this is my view. I didn't particularly discuss it with anyone -- well, I don't know if that is what General Perisic thought. That's what you asked me, whether he did or he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in that regard, we have seen earlier in the trial Exhibit P717, which is the letter from Perisic to Mr. Milosevic. You recall having seen that, where he's complaining about -- well, several things, but one of them is the failure to declare a state of emergency. Do you remember that letter from July of 1998 by General Perisic -- I mean, do you remember having seen it here in court?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In court, yes; but before that, I hadn't even heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1998 or early 1999 were you aware of it? Had you heard anybody in the army talking about it, that General Perisic had that disagreement with Mr. Milosevic about whether a state of emergency should or should not be declared?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really and truly, I did not even hear from anyone that there was a dispute between the Chief of General Staff and the president with regard to this matter. I didn't hear about that from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And in the Rules of Service it talks about how on the occasion of an attack by an insurgent terrorist, sabotage, or other hostile armed group, basically the commanding officer can immediately take the appropriate measures for defence and for repelling the attack. And that makes perfect sense to me, that you've got to have the right to self-defence when you're under attack. But my question for you, General, is: The operations or the actions in the summer of 1998 to the end of September 1998, what is referred to in some places as the five-phase plan to combat terrorism, those weren't immediate responses to attacks. Those were planned aggressive operations by the army against the terrorists, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were anti-insurgency actions of the police and Army of Yugoslavia on the basis of a decision made by the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some of those joint operations took place outside the border belt, that is, within the interior of Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The decision of the state leadership that you referred to in your prior answer, can you tell us specifically what document you're referring to. Is that one that we've seen here in court?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we saw here a document from the session of the Supreme Command -- Supreme Defence Council where the decision was taken to use the army to prevent the armed rebellion and terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija in case there is an escalation of terrorism. Then we saw special plans for combatting terrorism from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and we saw many, many orders from the 3rd Army, the command of the 3rd Army, for day-to-day engagement of the army in carrying out tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand right then, you were referring to the Supreme Defence Council minutes of the meeting in June of 1998 - I don't recall the specific date now - I think that was the 5th Session and -- where there was a decision that in the event terrorism escalated in Kosovo, the army should take appropriate measures or some language like that. That's the one you're talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I mean and I mean also what followed by way of the directive of General Perisic, Grom 98, 1 and 2. Those are the documents I meant initially and the document of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will come back to Grom 98 and some of the Grom 99 materials a little later, but let me continue on to something else at the moment. You mentioned that General Perisic called you I guess dozens of times when you were the Chief of Staff at the forward command post in 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the standard protocol in such a situation would be you would advise General Pavkovic about those communications from the Chief of Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and as for the entire composition of the forward command post during the usual meetings in the morning and the evening, I informed them that the Chief of General Staff called and inquired about such and such a thing, and of course it is only natural that I report to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've heard evidence in this trial earlier from some witnesses who have told us that on one or more occasions General Pavkovic may have skipped a step in the chain of command and gone to directly contact Mr. Milosevic. Were you aware of that in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, indeed, not in a single -- not on a single occasion did I have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this trial the first time you ever heard that suggestion made?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard statements, not assertions exactly, I have to admit. I heard that some people said that they either heard from someone else or saw for themselves -- well, I remember that sort of, but I do not remember any assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You talked early on about the distinction between joint operations and combined operations. At page 17788 you mentioned that the Law on Defence deals with the issue of combining not only combat operations but other forms of armed and non-armed resistance, that's Exhibit P985. Do you know where specifically where in the Law on Defence that subject is referred to and talked about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 16 I think, if I remember correctly at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you also mention in relation to that topic of combined command post I think in a discussion with Judge Bonomy you said you were using the official terms from the combat rules and manuals. Are those something separate and distinct from the VJ Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia do not contain provisions pertaining to command posts, command. What I talked about is most directly contained in the instructions for the work of commands and staffs, what a command post is, how it is established, types of command posts, the way in which tasks are carried out, all of that is contained in those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't recall, General, is that a document, is that an exhibit in this case?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a Prosecution exhibit, Mr. Prosecutor, it is a red manual -- it's two books, actually. I have information that that is a Prosecution exhibit, but I really don't know what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sometimes, General, I have difficulty finding some things because the -- the translation may not always be precise or consistent. I'll visit that later perhaps. But you were aware of those -- that terminology in 1998 and 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you, I don't understand what you mean. What terminology of 1998 and 1999? Or perhaps the interpretation is wrong. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was referring to your testimony at page 17789 where you said: "The official terms, Your Honour, are" - and you'll have to forgive my pronunciation are "objedinjena," combined command post, combining combat operations, combining other forms of armed or non-armed resistance, so these are the official terms that are used: "Objedinjena" and "objedinjena komando mesto," combined command post, which for all intents and purposes is the"objedinjena komanda," or combined command." That is the terminology I was referring to and you were aware of that and familiar with it in 1998 and 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand what the question relates to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit 5D424.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document we looked at last week when you were on direct examination from the Supreme Command Staff from the air force and air defence administration, and it's dated the 15th of May, 1999. And you told us about this and you explained that this was a proposal on how to coordinate and combine the operations of the army in terms of anti-aircraft defence in Kosovo that were placed under the command of two strategic groups, the 3rd Army and the air force and air command. Do you recall your evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you explained that, for example, at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, which was also your command post for the Pristina Corps, contemporaneously the forward command post of the air force and the anti-air defence, they were located there as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to say more specifically that it's the forward command post of the air force corps of the command of the anti-air defence. It is not the forward command post of that particular branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that help you, Mr. Hannis? There's -- I think there's a problem in that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm trying to sort that out, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It depends how important it is to you and what it is you're trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to make the point, General, that you said the commander of the army couldn't order that forward command post of the air force corps to support him. He could only ask or propose. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain for me how -- what the relationship was between the air force and the anti-aircraft defence with the VJ. Are not both of those under the General Staff and the Chief of General Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd Army is a strategic group within the army, the land forces, the air force is a strategic group under the General Staff, as a separate branch. Relations are on the basis of laws and regulations, but in terms of execution of tasks, such specific ones, what was ordered was to combine the activities, whereas everyone commands their own forces, which is quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in Pristina during the war, neither you nor General Pavkovic could request the air force to support you, but rather, that had to come from a higher -- well, you couldn't order them to support you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. We could not order them. We are not their superiors. We could only request, ask, propose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you had information or you saw a NATO bomber coming towards your headquarters, you couldn't order the anti-aircraft defence unit there with you to do something about it? You could only request or, what, go up to General Ojdanic and ask him to order the anti-aircraft defence to take some action? That seems a rather cumbersome way to operate, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the honourable Trial Chamber, this is way to simplified, and that's not the way it is. It's not the way it works. I say no, and if the Trial Chamber allows me to explain -- well, I don't want to be reprimanded, but that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the air force and anti-air defence that are in the area of Kosovo and Metohija within the general tasks of the defence of the country have their own defined tasks and they carry out these tasks from the point of view of air defence according to the tasks that they have from their superior command. As you can see, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff is turning our attention to this that the activities should be more combined at the lower level of troops in the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army with this other component of air defence, but only from the point of view of this coordination, not that someone would command somebody else. That is the essence of this combining without resubordination, although it's all the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this is dated the 15th of May, 1999. We know that, oh, about a month before this date that General Ojdanic was aware of the existence of the Supreme Command -- or of the Joint Command by virtue of his suggestions in P1487. Do you know why there wasn't a suggestion that there be some sort of Joint Command between the army and the air force or the air defence for this particular situation? Wouldn't it have worked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, speculation is called for here on the basis of Mr. Hannis's assumption that General Ojdanic was aware of the existence of some kind of a Joint Command and General Lazarevic is asked to speculate here based on the information that is not reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't have the precise citation right now, but I know that we have General Ojdanic referring to the Joint Command in at least one of the VJ collegium meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the contention. The contention is that Mr. Lazarevic isn't in a position to answer this question. It's something for higher up the ladder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understood his objection, Your Honour, is that I was asking the general to speculate that General Ojdanic was aware of the existence of the Joint Command, and I think we do have evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that your objection, Mr. Bakrac, that -- I now do understand what it is if it was based on the reference what General Ojdanic was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the basis of this speculation, General Lazarevic is asked to speculate even further as to why General Ojdanic did not figure out that a Joint Command should be set up between the Pristina Corps and the air force corps. He doesn't know what General Ojdanic knew, and I think that this is mere speculation on the part of the Prosecution themselves on the basis of a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no substance in the objection based on the lack of evidence of General Ojdanic having knowledge of Joint Command. There is evidence from which that might be inferred. On the other hand, there may be substance in the suggestion that Mr. Lazarevic is in no position to tell us why the Chief of the General Staff didn't make this suggestion. It wasn't how I read the question, but if that's what you're asking then it's beyond his knowledge, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I take your point, Your Honour. Let me rephrase the question and see if this is something General Lazarevic might address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your explanations about combined command and combined command post versus a Joint Command or a Joint Command post, in this situation where you have the air force and the army, which are both under the same superior, that is, the General Staff and General Ojdanic as the Chief of General Staff, couldn't a Joint Command function for coordinating those two separate bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a statement contained in this question, and that General Lazarevic confirmed that there was a Joint Command with a Joint Command post; and then a distinction is made whether this is possible is asked at all. General Lazarevic said, and we heard it dozens of times, that there was no Joint Command and that there was no Joint Command post. And now it is stated here that the Joint Command post and the Joint Command actually existed. I really fail to understand how many times does he have to say that in 1999 such a thing did not exist, how many times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was talking in a generic sense about his description of what a Joint Command would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you know that his description of what a Joint Command would be involves separate commands of the MUP and the VJ, in spite of the way you would seek to have it interpreted. You're wallowing here because you're introducing factors you don't need to, to ask the question which you want to ask, and your simple question seems to me to be: Because they both fall under the umbrella of the VJ, could a Joint Command not have been established to command the two together?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So all the other stuff really isn't necessary I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you've heard what Judge Bonomy just said. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff in this document, in no uncertain terms and in accordance with the Rules of Service, ordered that the operations for the troop anti-aircraft defence which was part of the air force and air defence should be combined. This is what the combat rules envisage. They do not envisage any joint of command, and this is the proper measure. This is the proper way and a fine example of how combat operations are to be combined, and this is what he ordered and this is the way we understood it during the war, how we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And General Ojdanic had the authority to order both the VJ and the air force, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but this is all the army. Could I be more specific? So he can command both the 3rd Army, that's the land forces, the army; and the air force. We are now -- we have a technical problem. It is much broader, and it would take us too much time to explain that in this courtroom. The air force is commanded from an operations centre where the situation in the entire air-space, not just above the country but even in the broader region, is controlled; and the commander does not have a this picture which would enable him to use the force of the air force. He has the forward command post of the air force corps. He is monitoring things, and he tells the general: This can be done, this cannot be done. And in the brigades there are air force officers who monitor also surveil the situation, they spot, and this goes down to the tactical level and this actually is functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that regard it was my understanding that there were some anti-aircraft air defence elements or assets that were integral parts of the units like the brigades; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Every unit has its anti-aircraft unit, which is the artillery battalion size, and it provides anti-aircraft defence for that unit. The corps has its anti-aircraft brigade, and the air force has its rocket anti-aircraft regiment, it has an air force regiment, and other units that provide anti-aircraft cover in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those elements, those anti-aircraft elements that were part of the Pristina Corps and the subordinate brigades, were army units that were part of your chain of command, correct? They weren't under the air force?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Those were units of the Pristina Corps which were part of the subordinate brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to move to Exhibit 5D99. These are the minutes of the 17th August meeting of the subordinate commanders with the forward command post. Do you recall this document when you testified earlier, General?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it, and I think I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down, I think there's a reference where it refers to the Pristina Corps commander reporting on the daily activities of the units in which the MUP was supported by the 15-3 combat group taking the village of Jasic and Djocaj. That may be on the next page. I don't know if it's on your B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not the right page and that is why the witness is unable to follow. Could we please ask for the next page to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to that you explained to us that this completed -- I'm at page 17806- this completed the circle in the execution of this task from the army commander to the General Staff down to the combat group, and now again the Pristina Corps commander informs the 3rd Army commander, General Samardzic, that the task had been carried out. And, General, are you aware that this was a matter that was discussed or advised about in the Joint Command meeting on the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I commented only on this event here, and I confirmed that the corps commander had informed the army commander about the completed actions to Voksa, Jasic, Djocaj, that's all one next to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us before that you recalled attending I think one meeting in August and a couple of meetings in September of 1998 of the group that we've been calling -- I've been called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the meeting you attended in August?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we'll show you all those meetings I think tomorrow because it's late in the day today. I want to move on to something else before I do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 4D377.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, this is an order from General Samardzic dated the 29th of May, 1998, and you pointed out to us as an example of how General Samardzic had issued an order that no element of the army could be used without his permission. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that, but can I please have it in Serbian -- oh, yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I note the date on that is the 29th of May, 1998, that was -- that was prior to the arrival of Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, Mr. Matkovic, and any record of meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all the details that you just listed here, who arrived when. I heard evidence from witnesses here, but I don't remember what the people said. But I can confirm this: I do know this time and I know where MUP actions were conducted in late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go next to Exhibit 4D091.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this relates to the question that you were asked last week by Mr. Bakrac about whether the 3rd Army commander used the term "Joint Command," whether you had ever heard him use that term. I think your answer was you didn't hear him use that term.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 I saw General Samardzic dozens of times, and I never heard him say that. And in the documents that are shown here, I saw that he, or rather, those documents from the army command used this term. I think that even General Perisic as the Chief of the General Staff mentions this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see in this document, 4D091, in item 3 it says: "The commander of the Pristina Corps as a member of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall attend all meetings." And as the Chief of Staff for General Pavkovic, you were not aware in late July 1998 that he was attending meetings of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, I knew that the corps commander has -- had meetings, coordination meetings, with the MUP staff in Pristina. I had information that those meetings of theirs between the army and the police were attended by some state officials, that those meetings were attended by somebody from the army command. And I knew that the corps commander would sometimes go to Belgrade to attend some meetings with the army commander. So this is the kind of information that I did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say you had information that -- or you said you know that he had meetings, coordination meetings. Who told you those were coordination meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, when he came to the forward command post to tour the units, told me that they had had meetings with the MUP members to exchange information particularly about the border area, to exchange experiences. And once the order had come from the General Staff and from the 3rd Army, to coordinate combat activities that had been ordered by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he not also tell you that there were civilians attending those meetings, in particular Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, did he not mention that to you as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander did not explain to me who was involved later at these meetings, who attended them individually. When I came to Pristina on two occasions, I, myself, was in a situation to see some of these persons, talk to them, exchange information. He never told me that he was going to a meeting where such and such a person would be because that changed too, I mean as far as I know. It wasn't the same people all the time, it wasn't always the same people from the previous period, too, it changed as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis you will see at line 11 the witness has already said that the meetings were attended by some state officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear him -- did you hear General Pavkovic use the term "Joint Command" in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really never heard him use that term, except that in some documents I saw this expression, the sentences, the letterhead. I explained what it was that I thought, but I never talked about it and he never said to me what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first meeting you attended in August of 1998, how did it come about that you attended that meeting? You told us you went to Pristina. Were you asked to come there specifically for the purpose of attending such a meeting or were you in town for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no other reason. I reported to the corps commander. I cannot remember what the specific task was, why I came for one day from the forward command post. We worked during the course of the day. In the evening he said -- well, I think it was the provisional Executive Council, that building, to see these colleagues from the police, to talk, and that's where I saw this group of people that I described, without remembering exactly who was there individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did he tell you when he -- I gather he asked you to come along to the meeting with him. What did he say about where you were going, who was meeting? He didn't mention a name of this group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, never. Quite simply, he said, We're going - he'd use my nickname to address me - he said we're going to such and such a place. And I would say, Yes, sir, and that was it. It's not that official, but when I saw, I saw those people there. I was glad to see these people, to hear something, and to go back to Djakovica then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we next look at Exhibit P1419.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, when he asked you to come along, you didn't inquire as to where you were being taken?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from our soldierly point of view, it's a bit improper, if the commander says, We're going, we go. I don't ask him where it is we're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Exhibit P1419, this is the 1st of August, 1998, from General Pavkovic to the 3rd Army forward command post requesting approval to launch the third stage of the plan to curb terrorism in Kosovo, and he makes reference to a decision at a meeting of the Joint Command on the 31st of July. As of the 1st of August, were you aware of the existence of something called the plan to curb or combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? As Chief of Staff, this seems like something that you would have known about.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the plan for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was made and approved, but I kindly ask the Trial Chamber, as for this constant emphasis on Chief of Staff, that I was really in a bit of a special situation. At a separate -- on a separate assignment, if I was in Pristina, I certainly would have known more about it. But really, I did have this separate task that I was working on, but I confirm this that I did know that at the level of the state, at the level of the General Staff, of the 3rd Army, of the corps, there was a plan for curbing terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And next can we see Exhibit P1423. General, this next one is dated the 7th of August, 1998, apparently from the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade. It's a report on combat tasks carried out to the command of the Pristina Corps, and it's talking about: "Between the 25th of July and the 6th of August, 1998, MUP units were engaged by decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Were you not aware by the 7th of August about joint operations being conducted pursuant to a decision of the Joint Command? Is this not a kind of document or a kind of information that would have been shared with you in the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written on this document who it is submitted to. With the leave of the Trial Chamber, I really wouldn't make any comments on this last point. Furthermore, this is an answer of the brigade commander to the request and order of the corps commander from the first sentence. That is to say that the brigade commander is reporting to the corps commander. As for this mention here in the text of the decision of this Joint Command, this order, those are the unsigned documents that have the function of coordinating activities between the army and the police, instead of having a plan of coordinated action or a plan of combining. That is the essence. We see here quite decidedly that the brigade commander is not reporting to some Joint Command whose tasks he had carried out; rather, he is reporting to his corps commander. That is the essence of my own understanding of this document and of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do have to stop, I'm afraid, at this stage and adjourn until tomorrow. As you now know, we shall add half an hour to tomorrow's hearing. The purpose of tomorrow's half an hour is to deal with a couple of administrative matters. We will conclude the evidence as usual around this time. So that's at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 24
